title: Problem Overview
content: Erdős Problem #1140 asks whether infinitely many n exist such that n - 2x² is prime for all x with 2x² < n. The answer is NO: Epure and Gica (2010) proved only finitely many such n exist. The complete list is {2, 5, 7, 13, 31, 61, 181, 199} with at most one additional exception in the n ≡ 3 (mod 4) case.
mathContext: Define $\texttt{AllShiftsArePrime}(n) \iff \forall x \in \mathbb{N},\; 2x^2 < n \implies n - 2x^2 \text{ is prime}$. The number of constraints grows as $\lfloor\sqrt{n/2}\rfloor$, so for large $n$ we need $\sim \sqrt{n/2}$ values to simultaneously be prime — a condition that becomes exponentially unlikely by the prime number theorem ($\Pr[k \text{ prime}] \approx 1/\log k$).

title: Imports and Namespace
content: Imports Nat.Prime.Basic for primality, Nat.Basic for arithmetic, and Finset.Basic for the finite set of known values. The namespace Erdos1140 scopes all definitions.
mathContext: The formalization uses Mathlib's $\texttt{Nat.Prime}$ predicate: $p$ is prime iff $p \geq 2$ and its only divisors are $1$ and $p$. The $\texttt{Finset}$ type provides decidable membership for the known values $\{2, 5, 7, 13, 31, 61, 181, 199\}$.

title: AllShiftsArePrime
content: AllShiftsArePrime n means n - 2x² is prime for every x with 2x² < n. For n = 13: x ∈ {0, 1, 2} gives 13, 11, 5 — all prime. The constraint 2x² < n ensures we don't subtract more than n.
mathContext: The predicate $\forall x : \mathbb{N},\; 2x^2 < n \to \texttt{Nat.Prime}(n - 2x^2)$ quantifies over $x \in \{0, 1, \ldots, \lfloor\sqrt{(n-1)/2}\rfloor\}$. Note $x = 0$ gives $n$ itself, so $n$ must be prime. The quadratic shifts $n, n-2, n-8, n-18, n-32, \ldots$ must ALL be prime simultaneously — an extremely restrictive joint condition.

title: KnownValues
content: The known values satisfying AllShiftsArePrime: {2, 5, 7, 13, 31, 61, 181, 199}. These were found by exhaustive computation and proved to be (essentially) complete by Epure-Gica.
mathContext: The set $\{2, 5, 7, 13, 31, 61, 181, 199\}$ has a striking pattern: the gaps $3, 2, 6, 18, 30, 120, 18$ are irregular, and the values are all prime (since $x = 0$ forces $n$ to be prime). The largest value $199$ requires checking $x \in \{0, \ldots, 9\}$: $199, 197, 191, 181, 167, 149, 127, 101, 71, 37$ — all prime.

title: n = 2 Verified
content: Computationally verified: only x = 0 applies (since 2·1² = 2 ≮ 2), and 2 - 0 = 2 is prime. The proof uses simp to simplify the constraint and omega to close the goal.
mathContext: For $n = 2$: the only $x$ with $2x^2 < 2$ is $x = 0$, giving $2 - 0 = 2$ which is prime. The proof is $\texttt{simp at hx; omega}$: first simplify $2 \cdot x^2 < 2$ to $x = 0$, then close by $\texttt{omega}$.

title: n = 5, 7, 13 Verified
content: Three more verified cases using interval_cases (which enumerates all valid x) and decide (which checks primality by computation). n=5: {5,3}; n=7: {7,5}; n=13: {13,11,5} — all prime.
mathContext: The $\texttt{interval\_cases}$ tactic: given $2x^2 < n$, derives $x \in \{0, \ldots, \lfloor\sqrt{(n-1)/2}\rfloor\}$ and creates one goal per value. Then $\texttt{decide}$ evaluates $\texttt{Nat.Prime}(n - 2x^2)$ by computation. For $n = 13$: $x = 0 \to 13$ (prime), $x = 1 \to 11$ (prime), $x = 2 \to 5$ (prime).

title: n = 4 Counterexample
content: Verified counterexample: 4 - 2·0² = 4 is not prime (4 = 2²). The proof provides x = 0 as witness, uses simp to compute 4 - 0 = 4, and derives a contradiction from the assumption that 4 is prime.
mathContext: The proof is by contradiction: assume $\texttt{AllShiftsArePrime}(4)$, instantiate with $x = 0$ (since $0 < 4$) to get $\texttt{Nat.Prime}(4)$, then $\texttt{simp}$ reduces this to $\texttt{False}$ since $4 = 2 \times 2$ is composite. This demonstrates that not all $n$ satisfy the property — a warm-up for the full disproof.

title: Epure-Gica: n ≡ 1 (mod 4)
content: Axiom from Epure-Gica (2010), Theorem 4.1: when n ≡ 1 (mod 4), the only values satisfying AllShiftsArePrime are {5, 13, 61, 181}. The proof uses quadratic residue analysis modulo small primes to eliminate all but finitely many candidates.
mathContext: For $n \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$: the values $n - 2x^2$ cycle through specific residue classes mod small primes. For example, $n \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ and $x \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ gives $n - 2x^2 \equiv 1 - 2 \equiv -1 \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$. Combining residue constraints from primes $3, 5, 7, \ldots$ via the Chinese Remainder Theorem creates a sieve that leaves only $\{5, 13, 61, 181\}$.

title: Epure-Gica: n ≡ 3 (mod 4)
content: Axiom from Epure-Gica (2010): when n ≡ 3 (mod 4), only {7, 31, 199} satisfy AllShiftsArePrime, with at most one additional exception. The proof relies on Mollin-Williams (1989) results on class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields Q(√(-2n)).
mathContext: The case $n \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ is deeper because it connects to class numbers of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-2n})$. Mollin and Williams (1989) showed that if $n - 2x^2$ is prime for all valid $x$, then the class number $h(-8n)$ satisfies strong constraints. By Siegel's theorem, $h(-D) \to \infty$ as $D \to \infty$, so only finitely many $n$ can satisfy these constraints. The 'at most one exception' arises from an ineffective constant in Siegel's bound.

title: Even Case: Fully Proved
content: For even n > 2: n - 2·0² = n is even and greater than 2, hence not prime. This eliminates half of all natural numbers. The proof extracts the x = 0 case, uses simp to compute n - 0 = n, then derives that a prime cannot be divisible by 2 and greater than 2.
mathContext: The proof chain: $2 \mid n$ and $n > 2$ imply $n$ is composite (the only even prime is $2$). Since $\texttt{AllShiftsArePrime}(n)$ requires $n - 2 \cdot 0^2 = n$ to be prime, we get $\texttt{Nat.Prime}(n)$ contradicting compositeness. Formally: $\texttt{Nat.Prime.not\_dvd\_one}$ applied to the prime $n$ and divisor $2$ (adjusted by omega).

title: Finiteness Axiom
content: The core axiom: ∃ B, ∀ n > B, ¬AllShiftsArePrime n. There exists a bound beyond which no n satisfies the property. This packages the Epure-Gica results (mod 1, mod 3, and even cases) into a single finiteness statement.
mathContext: Taking $B = 199$ (the largest known value): $\forall n > 199, \neg\texttt{AllShiftsArePrime}(n)$. This combines three cases: even $n > 2$ fail by the even\_case theorem, $n \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ with $n > 181$ fail by epure\_gica\_mod\_1, and $n \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ with $n > 199$ fail by epure\_gica\_mod\_3 (modulo the possible exception).

title: erdos_1140: DISPROVED (Fully Proved)
content: The main theorem: ¬(∀ N, ∃ n > N, AllShiftsArePrime n) — there do NOT exist infinitely many such n. The proof assumes infinitely many exist, extracts the bound B from erdos_1140_finite, finds n > B with the property (contradicting finiteness), and derives ⊥.
mathContext: The proof is a clean application of the Archimedean principle: assume $\forall N, \exists n > N, \texttt{AllShiftsArePrime}(n)$. From the finiteness axiom, obtain $B$ with $\forall n > B, \neg\texttt{AllShiftsArePrime}(n)$. Instantiate the assumption with $N = B$ to get $n > B$ with $\texttt{AllShiftsArePrime}(n)$. Then $\texttt{hB}(n)(\text{by omega})(\text{hn'})$ gives $\bot$. This is one of the fully-proved theorems in the file.
